seoTitle: Febrile Infant Workup by Age, Febrile Seizures and Kawasaki
metaDescription: The febrile infant and child for peds and EM rotations: the AAP 2021 workup by age in days, markers and LP rules, antibiotics, febrile seizures, Kawasaki.
h1: The febrile infant and child: the workup by age, fork by fork
dek: For the student on a peds or EM rotation with a febrile infant and a resident about to ask what is next: shock and seizures first, the workup at 8 to 21, 22 to 28 and 29 to 60 days, when the LP is needed, the antibiotics, the older child without a source, UTI, Kawasaki, febrile seizures, and what you will be pimped on.

shortAnswer.text: Airway, breathing, circulation and consciousness, then the vitals, a weight and the age in days. Shock gets crystalloid boluses and antibiotics within 1 hour; a seizure lasting 5 minutes is treated as status epilepticus.

shortAnswer.lead: Age in days sets the workup.
shortAnswer.text: 7 days or younger, or ill-appearing up to 60 days: blood culture, catheter urine, LP, count and CRP, then admission and parenteral antibiotics.

shortAnswer.lead: 8 to 21 days, well: the full workup.
shortAnswer.text: Catheter urinalysis, blood culture and CSF for every infant, admitted on parenteral antibiotics: ampicillin plus ceftazidime or gentamicin (AAP 2021).

shortAnswer.lead: 22 to 28 days: the markers decide the LP.
shortAnswer.text: Urinalysis, blood culture and procalcitonin with the ANC or CRP; an LP whenever a marker is raised. NICE still does an LP and treats every febrile infant under 1 month.

shortAnswer.lead: 29 to 60 days: no LP with normal markers.
shortAnswer.text: Normal markers and a negative urinalysis: home without antibiotics, reevaluated in 24 hours (24 to 36 in the AAP algorithm). A positive urinalysis alone is not a reason for an LP.
Abnormal in AAP 2021: procalcitonin over 0.5 ng/mL, CRP over 20 mg/L, ANC over 4,000 to 5,200 per mm3, temperature over 38.5 C.

shortAnswer.lead: Older than 60 days: vaccines and the traffic light.
shortAnswer.text: No source and no amber or red features in a vaccinated child: a urine test, not routine bloods, a chest film or oral antibiotics. NICE still tests every febrile infant under 3 months with a count, blood culture, CRP and urine.

shortAnswer.lead: Fever 5 days or more: think Kawasaki.
shortAnswer.text: Four of five features: echocardiogram, and IVIG 2 g/kg with aspirin, ideally within 7 to 10 days of fever onset. Two or 3 features with a CRP over 30 mg/L or an ESR over 40: the supplementary labs and an echocardiogram.

sections.heading: What do you do first with a febrile infant or child?
sections.intro: Airway, breathing, circulation and consciousness, then the full set of vitals, a weight and the age in days. Shock gets oxygen, access, crystalloid boluses and antibiotics within the hour; the LP waits until the child is stable.

sections.heading: Shock, seizure, purpura or age in days: which fork is this child on?
sections.intro: Perfusion, convulsions and the skin come first; then the age in days and the appearance pick the infant workup, and past 60 days the length of the fever and its source decide.

sections.heading: What workup does a febrile infant need at each age?
sections.intro: Every infant 60 days or younger gets a urinalysis and a blood culture. The full workup with an LP is for 7 days or younger, any ill-appearing infant, and every well infant of 8 to 21 days; from 22 days the inflammatory markers decide the LP.

sections.heading: Which antibiotics for a febrile infant, and when is acyclovir added?
sections.intro: Ampicillin with ceftazidime or gentamicin up to 21 days, ceftriaxone from 22 days for a UTI or no focus (NICE adds ampicillin or amoxicillin under 3 months), meningitic doses for an abnormal CSF, and IV acyclovir for any HSV warning sign.

sections.heading: Which febrile infants can go home?
sections.intro: A well 29- to 60-day-old with normal markers and a negative urinalysis goes home without antibiotics, with a safety net and reevaluation in 24 hours.

sections.heading: Fever without a source, a febrile seizure or 5 days of fever: what next?
sections.intro: Past 60 days: the vaccine record and the traffic-light features. After a febrile seizure: simple or complex, and signs of meningitis. After 5 days of fever: the Kawasaki and MIS-C features.

sections.heading: Does a child need imaging after a first febrile UTI?
sections.intro: The AAP advises a renal and bladder ultrasound after a first febrile UTI in young children; NICE images under 6 months, and later only for an atypical or recurrent UTI. A VCUG is only for an abnormal ultrasound or a recurrence.

checklist.heading: The well febrile infant of 8 to 60 days: what to send

items.text: In the AAP group: a rectal temperature of 38.0 C (100.4 F) or more, at home in the past 24 hours or in a clinical setting, born at 37 to under 42 weeks.
Urinalysis: a catheter or suprapubic sample at 8 to 21 days; from 22 days a bag or voided screen is allowed, with a catheter culture if positive.
A blood culture for every infant.
From 22 days: procalcitonin with the ANC or CRP; without procalcitonin, both the ANC and CRP.
CSF: every infant of 8 to 21 days; at 22 to 28 days if any marker is raised (NICE: every infant under 1 month); at 29 to 60 days optional with a raised marker.
HSV studies and IV acyclovir for vesicles, seizures, hypothermia, maternal HSV, CSF pleocytosis with a negative Gram stain, leukopenia, thrombocytopenia or a raised ALT.
Outside the AAP group: preterm, vaccinated in the last 48 hours, a focal bacterial infection, bronchiolitis or immune compromise.

rounds.present: Lead with the age in days, the appearance and the risk group, then the markers and the plan. For example: 35-day-old girl, born at term and healthy, with 6 hours of fever to 38.3 C, feeding well, a sibling with a cold; well-appearing and well perfused, no exclusions and no recent vaccines. Procalcitonin 0.2 ng/mL, ANC 3,000 per mm3, CRP 6 mg/L, catheter urinalysis negative, blood culture sent. Low risk for a 29- to 60-day-old under AAP 2021, so no LP and no antibiotics: home with warning signs, a way back and reevaluation in 24 hours while the cultures incubate. NICE would also test her with a count, blood culture, CRP and urine, keeping the LP for an unwell infant or a white count under 5 or over 15.

pimp.q: Why does a well 2-week-old get an LP?
pimp.a: Every guideline treats an infant under three weeks as at high risk of invasive bacterial infection. The AAP sends CSF in every well infant of 8 to 21 days, and NICE does an LP in every febrile infant under 1 month.

pimp.q: Why ampicillin in a febrile neonate?
pimp.a: It covers group B streptococcus and listeria, and cephalosporins do not cover listeria or enterococci, so ampicillin is part of every regimen at this age.

pimp.q: Why not ceftriaxone for a 2-week-old on IV fluids?
pimp.a: In a newborn of 28 days or younger it is contraindicated with calcium-containing IV fluids, and the label also bars it in hyperbilirubinemic neonates. NICE uses it only in term newborns over 40 weeks corrected and not on IV calcium.

pimp.q: Does a positive urinalysis at 6 weeks mean an LP?
pimp.a: Not with normal markers. In 25,374 infants of 29 to 60 days, meningitis was 0.25% to 0.44% with a positive urinalysis, no higher than with a negative one.

pimp.q: What makes a febrile seizure complex?
pimp.a: Focal features, 15 minutes or longer or stopped by medicine, recurrence within 24 hours, or a neurologic abnormality before or after. Simple is generalized, under 15 minutes and not repeated within 24 hours.

Fever for 5 days or more with 4 of 5: bilateral non-exudative conjunctival injection; a red mouth, strawberry tongue or cracked lips; a polymorphous rash; red, swollen hands and feet; a cervical node over 1.5 cm.

traps.text: Judging serious infection by the response to an antipyretic, or by the height of the fever after 6 months.
An LP before antibiotics in a shocked child. The LP waits; the antibiotics go in within the hour.
Letting the markers decide the LP at 8 to 21 days. Every well infant that age gets CSF.
Ceftriaxone with calcium-containing IV fluids in a newborn, or a cephalosporin without ampicillin when listeria is a concern.
An LP for a positive urinalysis alone in a 29- to 60-day-old with normal markers.
Oral amoxicillin for fever without a source, to cover a bacteremia the markers may have missed.
Waiting for vesicles before acyclovir in a febrile infant with an HSV warning sign.
An EEG, a head CT or routine bloods after a simple febrile seizure.

faq.q: Does a febrile infant under 28 days need a lumbar puncture?
faq.a: At 8 to 21 days, yes: the AAP sends CSF in every well-appearing infant, and NICE does an LP in every febrile infant under 1 month. At 22 to 28 days the AAP lets the markers decide, an LP if any is raised and optional if all are normal, while NICE still does one. Ill-appearing infants and those 7 days or younger get the full workup.

faq.q: What are the AAP 2021 inflammatory marker cutoffs?
faq.a: Abnormal: procalcitonin over 0.5 ng/mL, CRP over 20 mg/L, ANC over 4,000 to 5,200 per mm3 (the AAP gives both cutoffs), and a temperature over 38.5 C. Procalcitonin goes with the ANC or CRP when it is available; without it, both the ANC and CRP, with the temperature counted too. A raised marker puts the bacteremia risk over 5%.

faq.q: What antibiotics for a febrile neonate?
faq.a: At 8 to 21 days the AAP gives ampicillin 150 mg/kg a day with ceftazidime 150 mg/kg a day, both divided every 8 hours, or gentamicin 4 mg/kg every 24 hours; the US labels dose ceftazidime and gentamicin lower. For meningitis the AAP doubles the ampicillin to 300 mg/kg a day, where the US label keeps 150. From 22 days, a UTI or no focus gets ceftriaxone 50 mg/kg every 24 hours, with NICE adding ampicillin under 3 months.

faq.q: Can a febrile infant aged 29 to 60 days go home?
faq.a: Yes, when well-appearing with a negative urinalysis and normal markers: no LP and no antibiotics, with warning signs, a way back and reevaluation in 24 hours (24 to 36 in the AAP algorithm) while the cultures run. Hospital observation is the option when follow-up is hard. NICE leaves admission to the clinician and advises against oral antibiotics for fever without a source.

faq.q: Does a simple febrile seizure need a workup?
faq.a: No routine bloods, EEG or neuroimaging; check a glucose and find the fever's source. An LP is for meningitis signs, and an option at 6 to 12 months with incomplete or unknown Hib or pneumococcal vaccines, or after antibiotics; an Italian review recommends one under 1 year. About a third recur, 1% to 2% later develop epilepsy, and antipyretics do not prevent them.

An echocardiogram at diagnosis, and IVIG 2 g/kg over 10 to 12 hours with aspirin 80 to 100 mg/kg a day in 4 doses until afebrile for over 48 hours, then 3 to 5 mg/kg a day, ideally within 7 to 10 days of fever onset. A child still febrile 36 to 48 hours after IVIG gets a second dose. Incomplete Kawasaki is worked up with the CRP, ESR and an echocardiogram.
